questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to experience a culture vastly different from Denmark, and had wanted to revisit Japan for a longer period of time after my first holiday there.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: UTokyo sends a lot of emails with necessary information, and although there is a lot to look through, I found that it answered all of my questions to satisfaction.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I mostly received assistance in form of email, though I was made aware of the globalisation center on campus in case I had any questions I needed answered in person.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I lived at Mejirodai International Village, a dorm for UTokyo students. The facilities are very nice, but there is a long commute to both Hongo (25 mins) and Komaba (50 mins) campus. The social life at the dorm leaves something to be desired, as many of the domestic students are not very outgoing.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Check which campus your preferred courses are located at, and try to find housing close to those areas. Also, there are many more dorms than those connected to the University of Tokyo, that seem to have less strict rules about social life.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The website for registering for classes has a very bad layout and it is difficult to find the courses that you're looking for.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The first few weeks of classes you're able to sign up for as many courses as you like and swap between them. After the deadline, you're locked into your courses.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: We were able to ask questions to the professors in charge of the global program at the start of the term, and the office for global students was open throughout the registration period.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I registered for all of the courses I wanted, and switched one of my courses at the end of the registration period with no issue.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try out some different courses before you settle, and take into account which campus the courses are located on, what form of exam (if any) and other relevant info on the syllabus.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Note that it can be difficult to get credit courses in Japanese if you have no prior or a very basic understanding of the language

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found the courses fairly easy in terms of level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The flow between lecture and class discussion was much less strict at UTokyo, though the form was pretty set with few variations.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Comparative Analysis on Regional Organizations as Security Actors
Art and Feminisms in Japan since the 1960s
East Asian Thought
Multiculturalism in Japanese Society
Southeast Asia in Global Context
Earth System Governance
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Human Security-Southeast Asia and Japan in Global Society

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I think the Multiculturalism in Japanese Society and Southeast Asia in Global Context courses are both very interesting and give a good look into the region if you're interested in leaning more about Japan and of Southeast Asia

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You need to pay for national health insurance (about 300 dkk/month) once arrived in Japan, no matter if you already have health insurance and/or other insurance

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food at restaurants and convenience stores is way cheaper than in Denmark. Vegetables and fruit however are very expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The clubs and circles seem more catered towards domestic students and international students who are staying for more than one semester and already speak some measure of Japanese

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are clubs (serious endeavors with practice several times a week) and circles (more relaxed with 1-2 meetings a week) for a range of different sports and other activities such as book clubs, tea clubs etc. Note that most of these activities happen in Japanese.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: There is a group that sets up social events such as monthly lunches, parties and the like. A great opportunity to meet other students, local and international alike.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Going to Kyoto and Hiroshima are a must, as is seeing Mount Fuji up close.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I think it was a bit difficult to adjust to, as there are a lot of unwritten social rules that you need to figure out on your own

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: If you want to meet local students, you can either do it through circles and social activities. I didn't have a lot of classes with local students, but that probably depends on the courses you take

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: In public, it is frowned upon to loiter and be loud or eat/drink on the street. It can be difficult to find proper places to socialise with friends if your accomodation is strict about who is allowed inside.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Both the traditional architecture, such as temples, and the food are amazing!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Make sure to see parts of Japan outside of Tokyo, don't be afraid to talk to the people in your class (or outside of it), and make sure to keep track of important information from the univeristy/your accomodation/etc

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: a little bit of knowing japanese goes a long way, as most Japanese people don't speak English. If you can learn something before going, it will serve you well

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I met some amazing people that I never would have had the chance to run into otherwise. The people coming to study abroad in Japan are generally incredibly nice!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It requires a lot of energy to be in a foreign country so far from home, with very little opportunity to see friends and family. Furthermore it's draining to have to remember unfamiliar social codes and learn the motions of everyday life in a place so different from where you're from

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
